title: Effects of jump training on physical fitness and athletic performance in endurance runners: A meta-analysis
authors: Ramirez-Campillo R, Andrade DC, García-Pinillos F, Negra Y, Boullosa D, Moran J
population: Healthy endurance runners of any age and sex in controlled studies; 21 moderate-to-high quality studies with 511 participants
findings: Twenty-one controlled studies with 511 participants were pooled with a random-effects model (Hedge's g).

Jump training gave a significant moderate improvement in time-trial performance over 2.0-5.0 km (ES 0.88), without enhancement of VO2max, velocity at VO2max, velocity at submaximal lactate levels, heart rate or stride rate at submaximal velocities, stiffness, body mass or maximal strength.

Significant small-to-moderate improvements were found for jump performance, rate of force development, sprint performance, reactive strength and running economy (ES 0.36-0.73; p < 0.001 to 0.031; I2 = 0.0% to 49.3%).

The authors conclude that jump training is effective in improving physical fitness and athletic performance in endurance runners, and that the time-trial gain may be mediated by force generation and running economy.
limitations: The time-trial gain is for distances of 2-5 km, not for marathons or ultras; the abstract gives no dose (contacts, frequency or duration), no moderator results and no certainty rating, and it pools runners of any age and sex without a result by group. Abstract read; full text not read.
implications: Supports the plyometric half of the block in runners by a pooled analysis of jump training alone: better running economy and short time trials, no change in VO2max. A bodyweight programme of jumps is therefore not empty of evidence, and it should not be described as heavy.
Gives no starting dose, step or cap for ground contacts; the ladder keeps the 200 contacts of the earlier meta-analyses as its cap (A) and its starts and steps as defaults (D).
